chapter: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
title: Writing for the HRS label with Ellington sidemen and catching Duke's attention
summary: Jones recorded as a leader and writer with Carney, Hardwick, Lawrence Brown and others, which brought him to Duke's notice.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: For that group both you and Trummy were doing some writing, was that what you were telling me?
I wasn't doing too much writing. I was

doing more playing then. But I'll tell you during that time where I was doing a lot of writing, on a little small label called HRS, and let's see, who did we have, Harry Carney, Otto Hardwick, Lawrence Brown, Shelley Manne, Billy Taylor the bass player.
Uh-huh.
And that's -- oh, my writing got nominated for awards, yearly awards at that point.
Wonderful.

And that's when I first started getting associated with the Ellington outfit. And then Duke was a disc jockey on WMCA at that point, and he used to play the records, and he would call the personnel office and say, 'Hey, didn't those guys play with me once?'
(Laughter)
The band was under my name, you know. So we did -- we came up with some very good things. And then another time we'd rotated and the band was under Harry Carney's name.
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah, I think I have some of those 78s.
Yeah, they're old 78s, you know?
Uh-huh.
And I was writing the music and writing the arrangements and the songs.
Was Rex on some of those, too?
He might have been -- he wasn't on the ones I was with. Rex was on the HRS. He was doing some work there too.
I thought so.
But Joe Thomas, the trumpet player, was doing most of the stuff with us. I would have people like Joe and Lawrence Brown, and like I said, Otto Hardwick, Harry Carney. Ted Nash, who's out here.
Uh-huh.
Who else? I can't think. I can't think of who else. But it was a very good experience, you know?
Was that how you got -- Duke got to know you and your work, do you think?
I think so. Because there was nothing he overlooked.
Oh no, I know, he never missed anything.

Nothing he ever overlooked, never got past him, you know? And by me writing in that direction and having admired those guys, and then having those same men basically to be there, it made it right straight down the middle.
You were writing for the same sounds he was writing for.
Yeah, that's right, but you had to have those men to play it, you know?
